1971 Dodge Demon Looks Stunning in High-Impact Butterscotch, Packs the Best Engine
10 photos
Photo: Gause Garage/YouTube
In 2018, Dodge shocked the world with the Challenger SRT Demon , a drag-ready muscle car with an 840-horsepower engine. In 2023, the company took it up a notch with the Demon 170, rated at an incredible 1,025 horsepower. But the modern Challenger wasn't the first Mopar to sport the Demon badge.
The name actually goes back to 1971, when Dodge applied it on a version of the Dart. Introduced in 1960 as a full-size car, the Dart became an intermediate in 1962. It was downsized once more to compact dimensions in 1963, retaining its market position through 1976.
The Dart was redesigned for the fourth and final generation in 1967. Much like its corporate twin, the Plymouth Valiant, the Dart was offered in two-door sedan, four-door sedan, two-door hardtop, and two-door convertible body styles. The Demon arrived when Dodge decided to introduce a two-door fastback similar to the Plymouth Duster.
The coupe was initially supposed to be named the Beaver, but Chrysler's marketing department scrapped the name when it learned that "beaver" was CB slang for a part of the female anatomy. Instead, Dodge went with the Dart Demon. It was advertised as a performance model, and a Demon 340 variant was added to replace the Swinger 340.
The Demon was only available for two model years, and it sold quite well. Dodge delivered nearly 80,000 units in 1971 and just under 49,000 examples in 1972. However, only a tiny fraction of these cars were Demon 340s (10,098 in 1971 and about 8,700 in 1972). They're far from rare by production numbers alone, but restored examples in excellent condition are hard to come by.
If you haven't seen one recently, this 1971 Demon 340 is one of those Mopars that has it all. It's finished in a high-impact color, it has the most potent mill available in a Duster, as well as a cool houndstooth interior.
The hue in question is called Butterscotch (or Bahama Yellow on Plymouth models) and was discontinued after the 1971 model year. It may not be the most desirable high-impact color, but it sure looks stunning on this Demon 340.
Speaking of the engine, the Dart became a slant-six and small-block V8 affair after the 1970 model year. In 1971, the compact came standard with an inline-six, while the optional 318-cubic-inch (5.2-liter) V8 provided up to 230 horsepower. The Demon 340 was powered by the range-topping 340-cubic-inch (5.6-liter) small-block V8, good for 275 horsepower.
It may not sound like a lot compared to what was available on the market in 1971, but we need to keep in mind that the Demon was lighter than a B-body Mopar, so a 340-equipped Dart was likely at least as fast as an intermediate fitted with a 383-cubic-inch (6.3-liter) big-block V8.
But you don't need to be a fan of compact cars to appreciate a fine classic. This Demon 340 is pretty much a concours-ready gem. Check it out in the video below.
